title: Arc vs Rc
narrative:
## Choosing Between Arc and Rc

Both provide shared ownership via reference counting. The difference is thread safety.

### Quick Comparison

| Feature | Rc | Arc |
|---------|-----|------|
| Reference counting | Non-atomic (fast) | Atomic (slower) |
| Thread safety | Single-thread only | Multi-thread safe |
| Send/Sync traits | Neither | Both |
| Memory overhead | 1 word (count) | 1 word (atomic count) |
| Clone cost | Cheap increment | Slightly more expensive |

### When to Use Rc

- Single-threaded applications
- UI code (single thread)
- Tree structures in one thread
- Any scenario where thread safety isn't needed

```xiom
// Single-threaded tree node
pub type TreeNode = {
  value: Int;
  children: Vec[Rc[TreeNode]];
}
```

### When to Use Arc

- Multi-threaded applications
- Shared state across threads
- Concurrent data structures
- Server handlers sharing configuration

```xiom
// Multi-threaded shared config
let config = Arc.new(ServerConfig{ port: 8080 });
// pass config.clone() to each thread
```

### Converting Rc to Arc

If you start with Rc and need thread safety later, you must recreate:

```xiom
// Cannot convert Rc to Arc — they're different types
// Create directly as Arc if you might need threads later:
let shared = Arc.new(data);  // future-proof
```

### Performance Guidance

- Start with Rc for single-threaded code
- Switch to Arc only when you need to share across threads
- Don't prematurely optimize — choose correctness first
tips: Rc = single-thread, Arc = multi-thread — same API, different safety guarantees
Arc is slightly slower due to atomic operations — use Rc when possible
Cannot convert between Rc and Arc — choose upfront based on threading needs
When in doubt, use Arc — it's safer and the performance difference is small
